purpose_of_this_fixture: Calibration fixture for C57a, the header-present case. A first-hand discovery call with an environmental testing laboratory, exported with a large participant header and a matching meeting-chat file. The header lists fourteen participants in three org sections: two of the fourteen are bots that the chat file names differently; four listed people never speak (one of them contributes only through the chat); two people who do speak are not listed at all (one shared a room and a microphone with the laboratory director, one joined late); the org sections misfile client staff (the approver and the safety officer sit under the parent group, a client project manager on a personal login sits under External, and the client's outsourced IT provider sits under the client); one listed attendee has no role string; one role string contradicts what the person does (titled Administrative Assistant, runs receiving); and the header carries an account identifier and a meeting identifier. The key asserts the repair: the header is treated as claimed and not observed, both listed-but-silent and speaking-but-unlisted are reported, side is assigned from behaviour and not from the org heading, the contradicting role is recorded as 'titled X, behaves as Y', the no-role attendee's role comes from his own words, the two bots are resolved across the two files and are never attendees, the chat-only attendee's figures are cited from the chat under her own name and never as the colleague who read them aloud, the two silent decision-shaped attendees are promoted to a risk row, and the identifiers are never quoted anywhere, including in this key. Underneath the roster defects the call is a strong discovery: R1 to R10 Met (R7 met-with-residual), R11 Missing, R12 Partial, a client-built bleed, a conditional upside kept apart, three excavated pains, and a Work Management build with proposals parked.
transcript_format: Two ASCII files from one meeting. transcript.txt: a block export with a header between two rules (title, recording date and time, duration, meeting and account identifiers, organizer, a participant list of fourteen in three org sections with dotted leaders and role strings, and a note on where speaker labels come from), then 214 turns, each as a label line 'Speaker Name   HH:MM:SS' (wall-clock start time, Central, no end time) followed by the text and a blank line. Turns run 14:02:15 to 14:45:35, about 5389 spoken words, ten labels: 'Consultant' and nine other names (eight client staff and the client's IT provider), two of which (Bartholomew Nkemelu, Anouk Verstraeten) are absent from the header. Client share about 67%; the longest own-side turn is 102 words (14:39:55). Cues: [laughs] x6, [crosstalk] x1, [breaking up] x1; nine ' -- ' breaks (seven self-corrections and the two around the [crosstalk] at 14:18:02), plus fillers and restarts inside turns. Timestamps are strictly increasing with no collisions. meeting-chat.txt: 'MEETING CHAT', the same title and meeting identifier, an export time, a fifteen-name participant line captured at export (it includes the late joiner and both bots under different names, and omits the unlisted room-sharer), then eleven messages as 'HH:MM:SS   Name' plus one text line. The header's recording date (Thursday 8 October 2026) is metadata, not roster: it is kept because the weekday-date pairs in speech (Wednesday the twenty-first, Thursday the twenty-second, the twentieth, January first) fit it. Locations in this key are 'HH:MM:SS Speaker Name (role)' for the transcript, where the role in parentheses is the behaviour-derived role and not the header string, 'HH:MM:SS Consultant' for our side, and 'chat HH:MM:SS Name' for the chat file. Every quote sits inside one turn or one chat message.
